SeqPack consistently achieved the highest byte reduction across all
tests, highlighting how granular configurability handles heterogeneous recommender features far more effectively than traditional,

Abstract

1

Ratings and reviews capture different aspects of preference, so
rating-based collaborative-filtering and review-based models may
disagree on a user–item interaction. Aggregate accuracy does not
reveal why they disagree or which user characteristics are associated with it. We examine whether this reflects discrepancies between users’ rating tendencies and review tone. We introduce the
rating–review scale gap (RRS gap), the standardized difference
between a user’s rating leniency and review-tone bias. Large disagreement alone does not identify the better model, whereas the
RRS gap is consistently associated with whether the review-based
model predicts above or below the rating-based model, with domaindependent strength. Such user-specific discrepancies may therefore
help explain model disagreement. Our source code is available at
https://github.com/alsrb9936/rating_and_reviews.

Review text enriches recommendation beyond scalar ratings [3, 6,
12]. Ratings summarize overall preference within a limited numerical scale, whereas reviews selectively describe particular aspects,
experiences, and attitudes. For example, two users may assign the
same rating to an item, yet one may describe it as offering good
value for money, emphasizing a positive aspect, while the other
may focus only on how inconvenient it was to use, emphasizing a
negative aspect. Conversely, users may express similarly positive or
negative experiences in their reviews but assign different ratings because of differences in rating standards or leniency. Thus, the same
rating need not correspond to the same review tone, and similar
review tone need not correspond to the same rating [1, 7, 10]. Ratinghistory and review-history models may accordingly assign different
scores to the same user–item pair. We study this disagreement as
an interaction-level model-selection region because aggregate error
can obscure where review-based prediction helps or hurts. Building
on work on rating–sentiment discrepancy [1, 4, 11], we examine
whether persistent differences between user-specific rating leniency and rating-conditioned review tone explain disagreement
between separately trained NeuMF [5] and ReviewOnly models.
We define their standardized difference as the rating–review scale
gap (RRS gap) and test whether it tracks the direction and benefit
of model disagreement.

Introduction

Repeat consumption is an important characteristic of user behavior
in e-commerce platforms. Users frequently revisit and re-purchase
previously interacted items due to needs such as replenishment,
familiarity, and ongoing consideration. In such settings, a substantial portion of user activity consists of interactions with items that
have already appeared in the user’s history [1, 2].

Despite this, recommender systems are predominantly evaluated

which implicitly emphasize correct prediction over behavioral relevance. In repeat-heavy environments, this creates a fundamental
issue: recommending a previously consumed item is often predictively correct, but not necessarily useful or appropriately timed.
As a result, models can achieve high accuracy by exploiting repeat
behavior, without necessarily improving the quality of recommendations from a user perspective. Existing evaluation protocols do
not distinguish between meaningful re-engagement and redundant
repetition [3]. Furthermore, they do not account for whether recommendations are delivered at appropriate points in time [4, 5]. This
can lead to an overestimation of model effectiveness in domains
where repeat interactions dominate [6].
The issue is particularly pronounced for sequential and
representation-based models, such as recurrent and Transformerbased architectures (e.g., GRU4Rec and BERT4Rec), which are
highly effective at capturing behavioral regularities. However, their
performance gains may partly arise from exploiting high probability repeat patterns rather than delivering behaviorally meaningful
recommendations [7]. While existing research has explored beyondaccuracy evaluation [8], questioned the reliability of interaction
signals [3], and distinguished repeat from exploratory consumption
[9–11], or jointly learn heterogeneous temporal user preference
patterns to improve the timeliness of recommendation [12], current
evaluation protocols still predominantly treat all correct repeat
recommendations as equally valuable, overlooking their behavioral
utility and timelines. This raises a central question for recommender
system evaluation: to what extent improvements in predictive accuracy reflect genuine recommendation quality, as opposed to the
exploitation of repeat behavior. To address this gap, we investigate
whether high predictive accuracy necessarily translates into behaviorally useful repeat recommendations. We further propose three
complementary evaluation metrics that quantify repeat utility and
temporal alignment beyond conventional accuracy measures.

Fashion e-commerce routes every shopper through the same fixed
category tree and reads a dislike as a permanent verdict. Both assumptions fail during exploratory browsing, where shoppers have

Related Work

Our loop descends from relevance feedback: Rocchio [15, 17] moves
a single query vector toward relevant items and away from nonrelevant ones, while the survey literature already identifies the
negative term as the method’s fragile component [16]. Exploratorysearch research holds that information needs evolve during the

depart on the semantics of the negative signal.
Session-based RSs [7, 18] learn next-item prediction from logged
sequences. Our method is an interpretable state assembled online
without session-level training, with recency weighting long established in recommendation [4, 6]. PinnerSage [11] demonstrated at
an industrial scale that a long-term profile is better represented by
multiple embeddings than by a single one. We deliberately keep a
single point for the session (see Section 3).
Negative feedback is informative [5], and state-of-the-art sequential RSs train with a “not-to-recommend” objective that durably
suppresses disliked items [19], the modern reading of clean negatives. Closest to our work, PMORS [8] decays negative-feedback
penalties according to a forgetting curve while learning a ranking
objective over a persistent user profile. To our knowledge, no prior
work drives exploratory navigation with a session-only, decaying
query point whose negative feedback is reversible by design.

Arguably, driving music discovery is one of the most important
functions of recommender systems; however, defining what characterizes discovery and determining what constitutes a successful one
are both nontrivial problems. Here, we argue that repetition offers
a valuable lens: when users discover a track they like, they typically listen to it repeatedly several times. In this work, we use this
pattern as an indicator to characterise the quality of successful discoveries. We also argue that familiarity is a fundamental part of the
discovery process. We therefore use different familiarity measures
to construct user profiles from long-term consumption logs and
assess their ability to predict discovery success. Our experiments
on listening data from a well-established music streaming platform
show that familiarity provides a useful signal for discovery prediction, with performance improving further when user and item
information is incorporated. Source code: https://github.com/hcaimms/discovery-quality-and-familiarity.

Recommendation algorithms mainly focus on providing personalized rankings based on previously consumed items. These predictions are typically optimized to deliver a one-time relevance experience, which is effective in domains with high content volatility
(e.g., e-commerce, news). However, in the music recommendation
domain, when users engage with new songs that they like, they
often re-listen to them several times, which is indicative of their
satisfaction. Among other factors that enable discovery in music,
familiarity plays a key role by helping users discriminate between
different genres, artists, and tracks, which compound their musical
preferences. Surprisingly, only a few prior works include them in
their modeling.
In this work, we focus on the predictability of the quality of discovery based on familiarity profiles built upon historical streaming
data. For this purpose, we provide a definition of the quality of
discovery based on repetitions of novel items and employ several
measures of familiarity to provide insights into their importance. To
this end, we perform experiments with data from ∼50k users from
Deezer, an international online music streaming platform. Precisely,
we perform several discovery quality classification tasks with different combinations of familiarity profiles as well as user and item
embeddings. Then, we compare these results with pretrained user
and item embeddings1 predictions.

Related work. Familiarity is a well-established driver of musical
preference: listeners tend to favor familiar tracks over unfamiliar
ones, both in radio contexts [17] and, more recently, in streaming behavior [4, 16]. Musical interest can be understood as a balance between predictability and complexity [5]: music that is too
unpredictable may be overwhelming, whereas music that is too
predictable may lack stimulation. Berlyne [2] formalized this as
an “inverted-U” relationship between arousal and collative variables such as novelty, complexity, and familiarity, whereby liking
increases up to a point before declining. This pattern has been observed empirically in music [1, 3, 8, 10], suggesting that recommendation should balance familiarity and novelty. We have previously
observed this effect at the track level: the probability that a newly
encountered song is listened to rather than skipped increases with
repeated exposure, peaks, and then declines as familiarity builds

Predicting Discovery Quality from Familiarity

It is not straightforward to define the quality, or utility, of a discovered song. We posit that a discovery event in which a song
is encountered but fails to generate meaningful engagement is a
weaker form of discovery. We therefore consider a “good” discovery
to be a new song encountered by a user that subsequently leads to
repeated consumption.
We define a discovery event as the sequence of completed streams2
performed by a user on a previously unheard song, starting from
its first exposure. An event is positive if it has at least 2 completed
streams within a 7-day window, and negative otherwise. For positive
events, we define the discovery quality as the resulting level of user
engagement, measured by the number of completed streams. Since
repetition counts can vary widely across users, we split them into
three positive classes, low, mid, and high, based on equal-sized
terciles of each user’s normalized repetition counts, alongside the
negative class of events with fewer than 2 completed streams.

We describe the PoliBaJukebox submission to the ACM RecSys
Challenge 2026 on conversational music recommendation over the
TalkPlayData 2 corpus. Our system implements a modular twostage pipeline: a first stage retrieves candidates from the full track
catalog using ten heterogeneous sources, fuses them with weighted
Reciprocal Rank Fusion (wRRF), and reranks with gradient-boosted
models; a second stage writes the reply through a two-pass, factgrounded LLM pipeline. Our central finding is methodological:
on this task, offline development metrics can move against the
blind leaderboard rather than track it, so components validated
offline routinely failed or regressed on the blind split. We trace
this to a large, measurable covariate shift between development
and blind sessions (an adversarial classifier separates them at AUC
0.937 from input-side descriptors alone); a standard correction for it,
reweighting training toward blind-like cases, lowers development
nDCG@20 yet is what let the ranker transfer. Under this shift, the
offline selection criterion itself must change, not just the model.
Our compliant submission achieved a composite score of 0.576
(nDCG@20 0.445), placing PoliBaJukebox in the final top 5. All
codes and weights are released for exact reproduction: https://

Proposed Methodology

Our system decouples candidate ranking from response generation
into two independent stages per session (Figure 1), operating natively over the full 47,071-track catalog without heuristic track-split
filtering or diversity padding.
Stage 1: Deterministic Recommendation (L1–L6). This deterministic funnel optimizes nDCG@20. L1 queries ten heterogeneous
sources using dialogue history. L2 fuses these via weighted Reciprocal Rank Fusion (wRRF) [4] into a 300-candidate pool. L3 extracts
a 300 × 37 feature matrix (e.g., recency, ALS dot-products). L4–L6
route candidates via a primary LightGBM LambdaRank model [13]
based on score margins, blending outputs in z-score space with a
CatBoost-YetiRank ensemble [9, 15] to yield the top-20 tracks.
Stage 2: LLM Response Generation (L7). Operating on the
top-1 recommended track, this stage injects catalog facts (tags,
year, duration) and runs a two-pass LLM pipeline (gemini-3.1pro-preview draft → gemini-3.5-flash critic) to produce a factgrounded response.

Abstract

1

The Netflix Prize challenged teams to improve movie rating prediction by 10% in RMSE—a target that shaped recommender systems
research for years. Twenty years later, we revisit this competition
armed with AI-assisted coding, deep learning, and modern hardware. Our initial hypothesis was that today’s advances—including
orders-of-magnitude faster compute, mature deep learning frameworks, and AI coding assistants—would make the 10% improvement
far more attainable than it was during 2006–2009. Surprisingly, the
task remains remarkably difficult, despite access to the original
publications, first-hand competition experience, and all of these
modern tools.
We present three contributions: (1) methodological advances—
including a best single model that surpasses the original competition’s strongest individual predictor with a simpler formula; (2) an
analysis of AI assistance at varying autonomy levels, finding that
controlled, human-guided use is far more effective than fully autonomous AI; and (3) evidence that modern deep learning methods
offer limited gains on this task. We publish our code base to encourage the community to revisit this benchmark.

The Netflix Prize (NP) competition [3] was a defining challenge for
the recommender systems community, spurring years of research
into collaborative filtering and rating prediction. Two decades after the competition launched, we revisit the NP task with a dual
objective: to push classical methods further and explore whether
modern deep learning methods—largely untested on this problem—
can contribute, and to examine how AI-assisted coding with large
language models affects the execution of a well-scoped machine
learning project.
Our initial hypothesis was that the 10% RMSE improvement target would be far more attainable today, given published solutions,
our first-hand competition experience, and modern tools and hardware. Surprisingly, as we show in this paper, this proved wrong:
the Netflix Prize remains a remarkably difficult benchmark.
The community has since recognized that rating prediction has
limited practical value for recommendation: ratings are missing not
at random [19, 29], making ranking by predicted ratings unreliable.
Nevertheless, 20 years after the most popular machine learning
competition ever—which attracted over 40,000 teams—the NP remains an excellent testbed for evaluating ML methodology and the
emerging paradigm of AI-assisted development, the two central
themes of this paper. We publish our full code base to encourage
the community to revisit this landmark challenge.

ABSTRACT

In this paper, we apply a particular machine learning model
called a determinantal point process (DPP) [4, 13, 22], which is a
probabilistic model of repulsion that can be used to diversify sets of
recommended items (e.g., lists of videos, books, or search results)
[7, 14, 20, 21]. One key aspect of a DPP is that it can efficiently score
an entire list of items rather than scoring each item individually,
allowing us to better take into account item correlations.
Implementing a DPP-based solution in a mature recommendation system is non-trivial. First, the training methods for DPPs
are significantly different from those used in typical recommender
systems [3, 12, 14, 20, 21, 26, 27]. Second, integrating the DPP optimization with existing recommenders is complex. One option
would be to retool the entire infrastructure in terms of set-wise
recommendations, but that would discard the large investment in,
and the sophistication of, the existing pointwise estimators. Instead,
we use DPPs on top of existing infrastructure as a last-layer model.
This allows the various underlying system components to evolve
independently. More specifically, for a large-scale recommendation
system, we build a DPP using two inputs: 1) pointwise estimators
from a deep neural network built for recommendations [9], which
gives us a high-precision estimate of item quality qi , and 2) pairwise item distances D i j computed in a sparse semantic embedding
space. (e.g., [19]). From these inputs, we construct a DPP and apply
it to the top n items in a feed. Our approach has the advantage of
enabling teams of researchers to continue to develop the qi and
D i j estimators simultaneously with our development of a set-wise
scoring system. We can therefore achieve our diversification goals
while leveraging existing investments in a large-scale prediction
system. Empirical results on YouTube show substantial short- and
long-term increases in user engagement.
Our contributions are:
(1) We offer a simple and effective procedure for set-wise recommendations by leveraging DPPs. We define a parameterization and learning algorithm for DPPs that makes use of
pointwise quality scores for items and pairwise distances
between items.
(2) We describe a practical and modular approach which can
be applied in the context of latency-sensitive, large-scale
recommender systems.
(3) We offer both offline and online empirical results verifying
that our approach improves recommendation accuracy on
top of a mature, large-scale recommender system.

we briefly review DPPs, then describe our current choice of DPP

Many recommendation systems produce result sets with large numbers of highly similar items. Diversifying these results is often
accomplished with heuristics, which are impoverished models of
users’ desire for diversity. However, integrating more complex statistical models of diversity into large-scale, mature systems is challenging. Without a good match between the model’s definition of
diversity and users’ perception of diversity, the model can easily
degrade users’ perception of the recommendations. In this work
we present a statistical model of diversity based on determinantal
point processes (DPPs). We train this model from examples of user
preferences with a simple procedure that can be integrated into
large and complex production systems relatively easily. We use
an approximate inference algorithm to serve the model at scale,
and empirical results on live YouTube homepage traffic show that
this model, coupled with a re-ranking algorithm, yields substantial
short- and long-term increases in user engagement.

INTRODUCTION

Online recommendation services often present content in the form
of a feed—an ordered list of items through which the user browses.
Examples include the YouTube mobile homepage feed and the Facebook news feed. The goal is to select and order a set of k items such
that the utility of the set is maximized. Often times recommenders
do this by ranking based on item quality—assigning each item i
a pointwise quality score, qi , and sorting by this score. However,
this is sub-optimal as the pointwise estimator ignores correlations
between the items. For example, given that a basketball video has
already been shown on the page, it may now be less useful to show
another basketball video. This is exacerbated by the fact that similar
videos tend to have similar quality scores. Unfortunately, even if we
build a good set-wise estimator, scoring every possible permutation
of the ranked list is prohibitively expensive.

ABSTRACT
Repeat consumption is a common scenario in daily life, such as
repurchasing items and revisiting websites, and is a critical factor
to be taken into consideration for recommender systems. Temporal
dynamics play important roles in modeling repeat consumption.
It is noteworthy that for items with distinct lifetimes, consuming
tendency for the next one fluctuates differently with time. For
example, users may repurchase milk weekly, but it is possible to
repurchase mobile phone after a long period of time. Therefore,
how to adaptively incorporate various temporal patterns of repeat
consumption into a holistic recommendation model has been a new
and important problem.
In this paper, we propose a novel unified model with introducing Hawkes Process into Collaborative Filtering (CF). Different
from most previous work which ignores various time-varying patterns of repeat consumption, the model explicitly addresses two
item-specific temporal dynamics: (1) short-term effect and (2) lifetime effect, which is named as Short-Term and Life-Time Repeat
Consumption (SLRC) model. SLRC learns importance of the two
factors for each item dynamically by interpretable parameters. According to extensive experiments on four datasets in diverse scenarios, including two public collections, SLRC is superior to previous
approaches for repeat consumption modeling. Moreover, due to
the high flexibility of SLRC, various existing recommendation algorithms are shown to be easily leveraged in this model to achieve
significant improvements. In addition, SLRC is good at balancing
recommendation for novel items and consumed items (exploration
and exploitation). We also find that the learned parameters is highly
interpretable, and hence the model is able to be leveraged to discover items’ lifetimes, and to distinguish different types of items
such as durable and fast-moving consumer goods.

streaming services like Prime Video, Netflix, Hulu, TikTok, and

are many methods [19, 40] for content personalization and recommendation, sequential recommendation models stand out due to

the next content for the user. Behavioral Sequential Transformers (BST) [4, 29, 43] play an important role in ranking systems,

user-specific, challenging negative examples, many studies choose
negative samples randomly or according to popularity [22]. This
reduces the model’s ability to identify false positives, reducing its
effectiveness in practical applications. Moreover, the fixed sequence

model struggles to rank titles that satisfy both immediate needs and
consistent interests. Furthermore, many ranking systems overlyprioritize click-through rate even if completion rate [42] is often
a more reasonable indicator of user satisfaction and recommendation quality and these systems also narrowly focus on immediate
next-item prediction [8, 21, 26, 32, 33]. Overcoming these issues
will help to develop a ranking model that better aligns with user
preferences and improves long-term engagement.

Sequential recommender systems are an important and in-demand area of research. These systems aim to use the order of
interactions in a user’s history to predict future interactions. The premise is that the order of interactions and sequential
patterns play an essential role. Therefore, it is crucial to use datasets that exhibit a sequential structure to evaluate sequential
recommenders properly.
We apply several methods based on random shuling of user interaction sequences to assess the strength of sequential
structure across 19 datasets, most of which are frequently used for evaluating sequential recommenders in recent top-tier
conference papers. Since shuling explicitly breaks sequential dependencies, we estimate their strength by comparing metrics
for shuled and original versions of the dataset. We propose three approaches for this assessment: a sequential rule method
and two more advanced model-based approaches. The proposed methods are easily reproducible and consistent with each
other. We also examine the impact of common preprocessing and postprocessing techniques, showing that they may afect
conclusions about the presence of sequential structure. Finally, we introduce a method for distinguishing between recencybased and order-sensitive sequential patterns and for assessing their complexity. Our indings show that several popular
datasets exhibit rather weak sequential structure.

We propose three complementary approaches to analyze the strength of sequential patterns. These approaches

comparing chosen metrics obtained from the shuled and original versions of the data.
The irst approach, based on identifying sequential rules, is model-agnostic and straightforward. We count and
compare the number of rules before and after shuling. If the number of rules remains nearly unchanged, this
indicates that most of them were present by chance rather than relecting real sequential patterns. In contrast, a
dramatic drop in the number of rules suggests that many of them represent true sequential dependencies in the
data. Two other approaches consist of training a sequential model and evaluating how the performance changes
in terms of NDCG@k and HitRate@k, and how recommendation lists difer in terms of top-K Jaccard score [30]
when the model is applied on original and shuled sequences. Since the results can depend on the model used,
we employ two diferent sequential models of varying nature: SASRec by Kang and McAuley [18] and GRU4Rec
by Hidasi et al. [14].

domains. We identify the datasets with weak sequential structure that are less appropriate for SRSs evaluation.

1.3

Industry Deployment and The Multi-Agent
Shift

Industry deployment is accelerating. OpenAI has integrated shopping agents into ChatGPT [2], Stripe is developing standards for
agentic commerce [6], and LangChain has deployed multi-agent
orchestration in production [1]. Major platforms including Walmart, Amazon, and Alibaba are experimenting with agent-based
personalization and fulfillment, representing a shift where agents
are no longer isolated recommendation engines but participants in
complex ecosystems.
This transition fundamentally changes system design. Traditional recommendation systems optimize for well-defined metrics—
click-through rates, conversions, session engagement—within a
single decision framework. Multi-agent marketplaces operate differently: coordination patterns emerge from local interactions rather
than global optimization, and sequential commitments compound
over time in ways that short-horizon metrics fail to capture.
Foundation models amplify both capabilities and challenges.
LLM-powered agents can engage in natural language negotiation [4],
use external tools [7], and adapt strategies through in-context learning [8], enabling conversational product discovery, multi-seller bundle negotiation, and real-time optimization. However, while we can
trace individual agent reasoning [8], we cannot predict which equilibria agents will reach, why certain coordination patterns emerge,
or how strategic behavior propagates across ecosystems.

1.2

Why This Workshop at WWW 2026

WWW uniquely convenes communities essential for principled
multi-agent marketplaces: recommender systems researchers (personalization, multi-stakeholder optimization), information retrieval
experts (ranking, discovery), multi-agent learning researchers (coordination, equilibrium), mechanism designers (fairness, incentive
compatibility), and e-commerce platform engineers (billion-user
deployments).
The recommender systems community has developed long-term
metrics and fairness measures but typically assumes centralized
control. The multi-agent learning community has expertise in coordination but often studies abstract games rather than production platforms. The mechanism design community offers principled
frameworks but assumes rational agents rather than learning agents
with emergent preferences. This workshop addresses gaps at these
intersections through cross-community collaboration.
WWW 2026 arrives at a critical juncture. Industry deployment
is accelerating, but foundational research remains fragmented. Establishing evaluation standards, interpretability frameworks, and
robustness guarantees now can shape deployment practices before
systems become entrenched. The workshop will produce a synthesis document summarizing findings, open problems, and research
directions.

Introduction

Traditional recommender systems often rely on multi-stage cascaded pipelines [4, 5, 28], which suffer from objective misalignment
and error propagation. Generative Recommendation (GR) [13, 26]
formulates recommendation as end-to-end sequence generation,
but industrial deployment faces two key challenges.
First, limited deductive reasoning capabilities. Existing GR methods [2] mainly learn inductively from observed behaviors, making
them weak at rare contexts and ambiguous intents. In e-commerce,
surface actions such as comparison or exploration may not indicate explicit preference, while real purchase intent often requires
context- and world-knowledge-aware deduction. Directly using
LLM backbones [3, 8, 16, 27] can provide such reasoning but introduces prohibitive online latency.
Second, the dilemma between multi-scenario adaptation and resource efficiency. Industrial platforms span diverse scenarios (e.g.,
feeds and shopping carts); training per-scenario models is costly,
while a unified model may suffer negative transfer. Prior advances
mainly target discriminative ranking via scenario-specific towers
or routing/gating [1, 17, 22, 23], leaving generative multi-scenario
recommendation underexplored. To address these challenges, we
propose OxygenREC, an instruction-following unified generative framework that integrates world knowledge for deductive
intent reasoning and enables scalable multi-scenario recommendation within a single backbone. Building on the earlier OxygenREC
technical report [7], this paper retains the instruction-following
backbone, including Fast–Slow Thinking, IGR, and Q2I, while significantly extending the post-training stage through MCTS-based
candidate search and JPO-based multi-scenario objective balancing.

Abstract

Keywords

User interest modeling plays a vital role in industrial recommendation systems (RSs). Existing generative recommendation (GR)
methods rely on single-step direct inference, which falls short of
deeply modeling complex and dynamically evolving user interest.
Recent chain-of-thought (CoT)-based GR methods attempt to address this, but either suffer from information loss during semantic
space transformation in explicit reasoning or yield uncontrollable,
homogeneous reasoning chains in implicit reasoning.
To this end, we propose M2 GR, a Generative user interest modeling method using a Multi-granularity Multi-objective CoT for industrial RSs. The multi-granularity chain first predicts coarse-grained
interests in parallel (e.g., item attributes like brand and category)
and then refines them into fine-grained interests, i.e., the exact next
click item. Building on this click interest, the multi-objective chain
further predicts more complex user order interest. This stepwise
implicit reasoning, conducted entirely in the item space, preserves
complete user behavior information while enhancing controllability
and diversity in interest prediction. Comprehensive offline experiments and online A/B testing demonstrate that M2 GR achieves superior performance, while exhibiting scalability and plug-and-play
deployability in industrial-scale RSs.

Introduction

Recommender systems (RSs) implicitly infer user interests from
user profiles and historical interactions to recommend personalized
items, and play a pivotal role in e-commerce [7], micro-videos [4]
and social media platforms [32]. Traditionally, RSs have primarily
relied on discriminative models optimized for Click-Through Rate
(CTR) prediction [10]. However, such models remain descriptive
rather than predictive — they simulate patterns from past behaviors
rather than proactively explore deeper user interests or anticipate
future intent [9]. The emergence of generative recommendation
(GR) paradigms has driven RSs toward more proactive and forwardlooking approaches [8, 29]. Yet, the complexity and rapid dynamics
of user interests pose significant challenges for direct forwardinference paradigms in fully capturing essential user intent [9, 23].
Chain-of-Thought (CoT) [27], extensively explored in Large Language Models (LLMs) to enhance understanding and reasoning in
complex tasks [13, 31], has recently been introduced into generative
RSs with demonstrated early promise [12]. These efforts generally
follow two directions: explicit reasoning, which transforms item
semantics into text to leverage LLMs’ inherent reasoning ability,
often at the cost of information loss [15, 25]; and implicit reasoning, which enriches user representations with multi-step reasoning
hidden states, yet faces challenges such as uncontrollability and
reasoning homogeneity [23, 30]. Thus, a natural question arises:

In the first stage, we pre-train the foundation model via next-item

the second stage, we introduce a multi-granularity multi-objective

through stepwise reasoning. Unlike previous work, M2 GR performs
implicit reasoning directly in item space to eliminate information loss
and ensures semantically distinct intermediate steps to avoid potential
reasoning homogeneity and enhance personalization.
Extensive experiments demonstrate that M2 GR delivers more

This section presents M2 GR, which follows a two-stage training

Semantic IDs (SIDs) are hierarchical item identifiers learned via
residual quantization, offering a promising solution to cold-start recommendation, yet their integration into discriminative recommendations remains challenging and lacks systematic investigation. We
present Pin-SCALE, a framework for optimized end-to-end integration of SID into dense retrieval in cascading recommender systems.
Pin-SCALE instantiates the principles through three technical contributions: (1) cascading pooling preserving residual quantization
hierarchy that outperforms common pooling schema and attention;
(2) engagement-aware tokenization that encodes collaborative signals to fully utilize both content and user engagement pattern; and
(3) multi-view contrastive learning that harnesses query-item and
item-item co-occurrence to align SID representations with engagement prediction. Through extensive offline analyses, we collected
systematic guidance and proved the effectiveness of Pin-SCALE.
Furthermore, the framework has been tested online on multiple surfaces at Pinterest including Closeup, Home Feed and Search, with
different content types like organic and e-commerce. Pin-SCALE
achieves substantial improvements in fresh engagements (+3.67%
repins) as well as platform-level retention (+0.05% DAU). Our work
has been shipped into production to serve billions of requests daily
and drive discovery journey of our users, as well as provides principled guidelines for SID adoption in discriminative recommendation
models at production scale.

Introduction

Recommender systems, which suggest relevant and engaging items
based on a given query and context, typically employ a multi-stage
process consisting of retrieval and ranking. The retrieval stage
selects a broad set of candidates from the inventory, which the
ranking stage then scores and orders. This work focuses on improving retrieval performance for fresh items, which is a critical
bottleneck: if relevant fresh candidates are not retrieved, they have
no chance of being shown to the user.
Such a cold-start problem is challenging due to lack of historical
interactions [1]. In particular, learning effective representations
(embeddings) for these new items is difficult. Embeddings generated from an item’s content (e.g., text and images) are available
immediately upon creation. However, content-only embeddings
inherently lack engagement signals that are crucial for predicting
relevance. Therefore, many state-of-the-art methods rely on training unique embeddings for each item ID on historical interaction
data [5, 6, 10]. While highly effective for established items, this
approach fails for fresh items that are not present in the training
set.
Recently, Semantic IDs (SIDs) have emerged as a promising solution for cold-start recommendation [12]. SIDs are unique identifiers
generated from an item’s content, which means they can be created
for fresh items immediately. Beyond serving as a semantic prior,
SIDs discretize an item into a small set (or sequence) of shared
semantic tokens, enabling parameter sharing across many items.

Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a critical task in personalized
recommender systems. Existing methods that align collaborative
information from conventional CTR models with semantic information from pre-trained language models (PLMs) have demonstrated
superior performance compared to approaches relying on a single
information source. However, most of them perform alignment at
the embedding level, which introduces noise from heterogeneous
vector spaces and limits fine-grained semantic mapping. Moreover,
these models highly depend on tabular features, thereby limiting
their transferability. To address these challenges, we propose to
conduct Multi-scale Graph Tokens Alignment (MGTA) for CTR
prediction via pre-trained language models, which enables deep
cross-modal information alignment while maintaining strong generalizability. Specifically, MGTA first captures multi-scale graph
tokens rich in collaborative signals by decoupling and quantizing
graph structures based on graph neural networks (GNNs), and
then achieves token-level alignment between collaborative signals
and semantic knowledge via PLM fine-tuning. To achieve efficient
transfer with MGTA, we further introduce the Cross-domain Token
Adapter that enables collaborative signals adaptation by mapping
graph tokens from the target domain to the source domain, which
necessitates only the injection of target-domain semantic knowledge, in turn reducing fine-tuning time. Extensive experiments on
three real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of MGTA
compared to existing baselines.

Introduction

Click-through rate (CTR) prediction is a fundamental task in internet services such as recommender systems [20, 72] and online
advertising [2, 9], as it quantifies the appeal of the content presented to users. The primary objective is to estimate the probability
that a user will click on a specific item based on historical behavior
[29, 63, 73]. The predicted CTR guides the platforms’ content delivery decisions. Consequently, accurate CTR prediction is vital for
capturing user attention and increasing platform revenue [16, 28].
Traditional collaborative CTR models convert raw input data into
ID features using one-hot encoding and model high-order feature
interactions to capture collaborative signals [5, 70]. It is worth
noting that although graph neural network (GNN)-based methods
are not directly applied to CTR prediction due to the high inference
cost of large-scale graph computation [4, 61], they still demonstrate
superior capability in capturing collaborative signals by modeling
multi-order user-item interactions [15, 32]. However, these methods
discard the semantic information in textual features and struggle to
capture semantic correlations between feature descriptions [7, 27].
The emergence of pre-trained language models (PLMs) has introduced a new paradigm for CTR prediction by leveraging advanced
natural language understanding to extract deep semantic relationships from textual data [30, 31]. The CTR prediction task is reframed
as a binary text classification problem by encoding textual sentences
via PLMs. PLMs’ capacity to comprehend textual information enables robust performance even with sparse user-item interactions
[26]. Nevertheless, they struggle to capture and understand collaborative signals because their fixed data-processing pipeline prevents
them from modeling relationships between users and items [33, 35].

In recent years, several studies have sought to align collaborative signals with textual semantics to leverage the complementary strengths of both modalities [27, 30, 55]. These methods typically adopt a dual-encoder architecture where ID-based models
and PLMs process tabular and textual representations of the same
input. To bridge the semantic gap between these heterogeneous
modalities, cross-modal alignment mechanisms are employed to
facilitate knowledge alignment. They typically optimize alignment
objectives designed to enforce cross-modal consistency, employing mechanisms that either encourage similarity between paired
representations or enable information exchange across modalities.
Through these alignment strategies, collaborative models can acquire semantic knowledge and external world information embedded in PLMs, while PLMs can better capture field-wise collaborative
patterns essential for recommendation. In summary, by sharing
representation spaces or introducing cross-view constraints, these
methods perform cross-modal information fusion and achieve substantial performance improvements in recommendation tasks.
However, the aforementioned methods also have certain limitations. On the one hand, single-scale collaborative embeddings are
insufficient to capture fine-grained collaborative signals at multiple
granularities, while multi-scale representations facilitate multi-hop
reasoning over interaction structures and reveal long-range dependencies. Moreover, fundamental differences in representation forms
and structural properties between collaborative information and
textual semantics persist. Therefore, embedding-level alignment
may introduce heterogeneous noise from disparate modality spaces,
compromising the alignment quality [68, 74]. On the other hand,
the heavy reliance on tabular features within individual datasets
limits effective transfer and generalization in cross-domain recommendation [34, 50].
To solve these challenges above, we propose to conduct Multiscale Graph Tokens Alignment (MGTA) for CTR prediction via
pre-trained language models in this paper. The core idea of MGTA is
to leverage graph tokens as a bridge between collaborative models
and PLMs for token-level knowledge alignment, while enhancing
cross-domain training efficiency. MGTA consists of two main stages:
(1) Graph Tokenization, where the user-item interaction graph
is constructed as a bipartite graph, and a GNN model is employed
to extract multi-hop neighborhood information from nodes. To
align collaborative structures with textual semantics, nodes’ collaborative feature representations are discretized by residual vector
quantization (RVQ) into multi-scale graph tokens, each representing
distinct interaction patterns and graph structures. (2) Token-PLM
Alignment, in which these graph tokens, serving as prefix states,
are input into the PLM alongside textual semantic information for
fine-tuning, enabling the PLM to model associations between collaborative graph structures and content semantics. Graph tokens

Recent advances in generative recommendation have leveraged
pretrained LLMs by formulating sequential recommendation as autoregressive generation over a unified token space comprising language tokens and itemic identifiers, where each item is represented
by a compact sequence of discrete tokens, namely Semantic IDs

large-scale item corpora and provides a natural interface for LLMbased recommenders to leverage rich world knowledge. Meanwhile,
breakthroughs in LLM reasoning motivate reasoning-enhanced recommendation, yet effective reasoning over SIDs remains underexplored and challenging. Itemic tokens are not natively meaningful

hard to evaluate, making high-quality supervision scarce.

Concretely, SIDReasoner first enhances
SID-language alignment via multi-task training on an enriched SIDcentered corpus synthesized by a stronger teacher model, grounding
itemic tokens in diverse semantic and behavioral contexts. Building

reasoning and latent reasoning. Explicit reasoning generates natural language rationales to explicitly articulate user preferences
[12, 31, 48, 62, 63, 66]. The latent reasoning improves efficiency

interpretability and controllability [11, 37, 46, 71]. However, representing items purely with textual descriptions suffers from severe
decoding inefficiency and item grounding issues, limiting its practicality in real-world systems [34]. A recent promising direction
avoids such issues by representing items with SIDs and expanding

in SIDs within a unified representation space [17, 38]. While this
paradigm offers new potential for reasoning in recommendation,
its effectiveness critically depends on the quality of SID–language

pretraining with substantial computational cost.

Modern recommender systems increasingly operate within mixedinterface ecosystems, transitioning users between high-intent browsing (e.g., Homepage) and low-intent browsing (e.g., infinite feeds).
While zero-shot distillation offers a cost-efficient solution for some
knowledge transfer scenarios, we demonstrate its critical limitations when source and target domains exhibit significant behavioral
heterogeneity or "intent gaps". Extending our prior work on zeroshot cross distillation, this paper presents a case study on adapting
a large-scale shared teacher optimized for high-intent (long-form)

and severe intent dissonance where the active selection signals
(clicks) from the teacher do not effectively map to the passive viewing signals (swipes/dwell) required by the student. To overcome
this, we propose a domain-adaptive approach implemented on a
multi-billion parameter model. First, we address label and covariate
shift by enriching the teacher with Shorts signals; second, we tackle
the practical challenge of increased distributional variance using
an optimized backbone architecture to effectively disentangle these
intent signals. The enhanced teacher yields significant gains in
offline and online metrics, establishing a blueprint for successful

scenarios where the user intent differs fundamentally.

such random augmentations might introduce semantic noise and disrupt the sequence structure and context.
For instance, an original sequence focusing on “consumer electronics” may shift to “cosmetics” after random
replacement. This misleads the model and weakens its ability to discriminate users’ true intent.
To overcome these limitations, we propose DiffCDSR, a novel CDSR framework that integrates conditional
diffusion models with mutual information-driven contrastive learning. Our approach addresses both time modeling
and pseudo-negative generation through the following two innovations: (1) A Position Re-weighting module
(PR) that learns user-specific decay curves to dynamically scale the influence of interactions—preserving longterm preferences while attenuating transient spikes. (2) A diffusion-guided contrastive learning strategy where
pseudo-negatives are generated via conditional denoising, ensuring deviations reflect plausible alternatives (e.g.,
replacing ‘Sci-Fi’ movies with ‘Fantasy’ books) rather than arbitrary noise. While diffusion models have been
used in single-domain recommendation (e.g., DiffuRec [3]), our work is the first to adapt them for generating
pseudo-negative samples in cross-domain sequential settings.

— We propose a learnable Position Re-weighting mechanism, PR, to dynamically adjust positional importance

of domains, and these strengths have also been increasingly evidenced in recommender systems. However,
existing methods that attempt to integrate collaborative signals into LLMs often fail to preserve their foundational knowledge. This loss is critical in text-rich recommendation, where robust semantic understanding is

framework that equips an LLM with recommendation capabilities while keeping its original parameters fixed.

mitigate popularity bias. Experiments on public benchmarks show that PALRec consistently outperforms fully
fine-tuned counterparts in recommendation accuracy while preserving the LLM’s pre-trained knowledge.

textual information in recommender systems.

Introduction

Recommender systems are the cornerstone of modern digital platforms, with sequential recommendation being a key task that models the dynamic evolution of user preferences [6, 46]. For years,
this field has been advanced by deep learning models, ranging from Recurrent Neural Networks
(RNNs) to powerful Transformers [9, 12, 15, 38, 41, 61], which excel at capturing dependencies in
sequences of item IDs. However, a fundamental limitation of these traditional ID-centric models
lies in their inability to leverage the rich, unstructured text associated with users and items, such
as reviews and descriptions [29]. This textual data provides crucial context and reasoning behind
user choices, which are semantic signals that ID-based models cannot access. The advent of Large
Language Models (LLMs) presents a new paradigm, bringing language comprehension and world
knowledge to bridge this semantic gap [46].
A common strategy for harnessing LLMs is to reformulate recommendation as a language task and
fine-tune a pre-trained model on domain-specific interaction data [1, 7]. While straightforward, this
approach poses a critical dilemma: fine-tuning can cause the model’s parameters to over-specialize,
leading to a degradation of the broad, pre-trained knowledge that made the LLM powerful in the
first place [23]. This issue can be problematic in text-rich recommendation scenarios, where robust
semantic understanding is needed to interpret reviews and descriptions and align them with user and
item identities. As illustrated in Figure 1, a model fine-tuned for product recommendation may lose
its ability to answer simple factual questions, instead producing overly domain-specific text. This
“knowledge degradation” undermines a key advantage of using LLMs, creating a pressing need for a
method that can integrate recommendation capabilities while preserving the model’s foundational
knowledge. This challenge motivates our work and leads to three Research Questions (RQs):
(1) RQ1. Parameter Preservation: How can we augment an LLM with specialized knowledge of collaborative patterns for sequential recommendation without updating its original parameters,
thereby preserving its invaluable pre-trained knowledge?
(2) RQ2. Semantic Guidance: How can we effectively process noisy, unstructured text (e.g., user
reviews) to generate high-quality, factually grounded semantic signals that can guide the
training of recommendation-specific modules?
(3) RQ3. Stable Optimization: How can we design an effective multi-task learning framework
for aligning collaborative signals (from interaction sequences) and semantic signals (from
textual data) in a manner that is stable and robust to popularity bias?
In this article, we build upon the ReLRec framework [29] and propose PALRec, a Parameterpreserved Augmentation framework for LLM-based Recommendation, to address the RQs. To answer
RQ1, we treat the LLM as a frozen backbone and introduce lightweight, trainable user and item
embedding modules. These modules are the only components updated during training, thereby
ensuring that the LLM’s foundational knowledge remains intact. While our work is inspired by the
prior parameter-preserving model ReLRec [29], we introduce a stricter augmentation architecture
that fully isolates the LLM’s original components, enabling better preservation of its generalpurpose capabilities. A detailed comparison with ReLRec is provided in Appendix A. For RQ2,
we design an Evidence-Grounded Profile Generation module, a hierarchical pipeline that distills
raw reviews into concise, factual user and item profiles serving as pseudo-labels for semantic
supervision. Finally, to address RQ3, we devise a multi-task learning objective that jointly optimizes
next-item prediction and profile reconstruction, thereby aligning collaborative and semantic signals
in the embedding space. To ensure stability and fairness, we further decompose token-wise losses
and apply a frequency-aware reweighting scheme to mitigate popularity bias.

gatekeeper for the item catalog. Embedding-based retrieval
is commonly used for this stage. Users and items are represented as dense vectors, and candidate items are selected
using dot-product or nearest-neighbor search. This search
can be implemented through different retrieval architectures,
including exhaustive SQL dot-product scans, external vectorsearch libraries such as FAISS, and database-integrated vector

Introduction

Large-scale pretrained multimodal embedding models are increasingly becoming reusable infrastructure for retrieval, ranking, and
recommendation, as they project heterogeneous item content into
transferable semantic spaces [14, 19, 23, 35, 40]. A recent stateof-the-art example is Qwen3-VL-Embedding, which demonstrates
the power of this paradigm by mapping text, images, document
images, and video into a unified representation space with strong

multimodal retrieval performance [24]. This is especially promising
for multimodal sequential recommendation, where the quality of
item’s modality representations directly shapes next-item prediction [18, 26, 41, 42, 53]. When the predictor operates on semantically
rich multimodal embeddings, it can exploit content continuity, semantic substitutability, and cross-modal expressions of user intent
in addition to collaborative signals [7–9, 33]. Stronger multimodal
embedding backbones should therefore provide a stronger foundation for sequential recommendation.
However, directly applying large pre-trained multimodal embedding models to sequential recommendation often leads to suboptimal performance due to domain misalignment [7]. These pretrained
embedding models are typically learned for general semantic representation rather than recommendation-specific objectives, while
sequential recommendation depends on user behavior, transition
patterns, and recommendation relevance that can differ substantially from standard semantic similarity [49]. Although end-to-end
adaptation can effectively bridge this gap, it is often impractical
for deployment because of its high computational and memory
cost [25]. This trade-off is especially important in sequential recommendation, where the same item encoder is reused over a large
catalog and efficient offline embedding extraction is often crucial
for deployment. This challenge remains significant not only for full
fine-tuning but also for conventional parameter-efficient tuning
when the backbone model is large [38]. In this setting, side adaptation [7, 9] is particularly appealing because it keeps the backbone
frozen while learning only a lightweight side branch, enabling efficient training, offline caching of item representations, and practical
deployment at scale, while still retaining strong recommendation
performance. Motivated by this promise, recent works have begun
to explore side-adapter-style designs for sequential recommendation with large embedding backbones [7–9, 45]. In this work, we
focus specifically on frozen, offline-cacheable item-side adaptation
of a unified single-tower multimodal embedding backbone. The resulting item representations are user-independent, while the downstream sequential model is treated as a shared component rather
than part of the proposed adaptation architecture.
Most prior methods [7–9] adopt a conventional side-adapter
design, in which a lightweight bottleneck adapter with a residual
connection is attached to each backbone layer to adapt its hidden
states. Although this paradigm is computationally efficient, we find
that its performance becomes suboptimal when extended to fulldepth adaptation, as shown in Figure 1. Existing studies [7, 8, 38]
observe the same issue and therefore treat layer dropping as a
default setting, since adapting more hidden layers can even degrade
performance.
We argue that this limitation stems from two key challenges:
(1) the lack of modeling of how fused representations are selected
during direct residual addition, and (2) the inadequate preservation
of earlier representations during progressive sigmoid fusion. First,
residual connection lacks modeling of what to retain or suppress
in fused representations. In side adaptation, the propagated representation at each layer is already a fused embedding of the current

Generative recommendation commonly represents items using
fixed-length semantic identifiers (SIDs) constructed through clustering and quantization. However, these artificial codes may overcompress item semantics, remain misaligned with pretrained LLM
vocabularies, and require costly autoregressive decoding. In light
of this, we propose VaLiDRec, a generative recommendation framework based on variable-length, LLM-aligned semantic identifiers.
VaLiDRec constructs SIDs directly from informative native LLM vocabulary tokens via token importance estimation, semantic-qualityaware pruning, and collision-aware refinement, allowing identifier lengths to adapt to item semantic complexity. To model user
preferences, VaLiDRec incorporates graph-aware soft prompts and
reformulates recommendation as token-set prediction with tokenlevel item scoring, eliminating autoregressive SID generation and
beam search. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that
VaLiDRec consistently outperforms strong sequential and generative recommendation baselines across all evaluation metrics. It
further achieves superior zero-shot item cold-start performance
and 87.49× faster inference than LC-Rec. These results demonstrate
that LLM-native variable-length semantic identifiers provide a more
expressive and efficient paradigm for generative recommendation.

Generative recommendation (GR) formulates recommendation as
a conditional generation problem, where the target item identifier or textual representation is generated directly from user interaction histories, contextual information, and natural language
prompts [7, 26, 31, 34]. Unlike conventional discriminative recommenders that rank candidate items using matching functions, GR
integrates user preference modeling, item semantic understanding,
and candidate generation within a unified framework. Leveraging
the strong language understanding and semantic modeling capabilities of large language models (LLMs) [1, 2, 8], recent GR methods
can directly exploit rich item metadata and pretrained semantic
knowledge, making them particularly promising for sparse, longtail, and cold-start recommendation scenarios.
Generating appropriate item representations is fundamental to
generative recommendation, as the output space must be both semantically expressive and precisely retrievable. Directly generating
raw item IDs [7, 14, 23] preserves one-to-one item mapping but
lacks semantic structure, making it difficult to capture semantic
relationships among items. In contrast, generating free-form textual
descriptions provides richer semantic expressiveness but results in
an open-ended output space, where generated content may be ambiguous, hallucinated, or difficult to align with items in the corpus.
To balance semantic expressiveness, controllability, and inference
efficiency, recent GR methods commonly adopt semantic identifiers (SIDs) [11, 19, 26], which represent each item as a sequence
of discrete semantic tokens and train generative models to predict
the target item’s SID. These SIDs are typically constructed using
clustering or quantization methods, such as RQ-KMeans [4], RQVAE [17], and FSQ [22], to encode item similarity into a structured
output space. Consequently, SIDs have emerged as an effective
interface between generative sequence modeling and large-scale
item retrieval.
However, existing SID-based methods still exhibit three major limitations. First, most SIDs are constructed by clustering or
quantizing continuous item representations into artificial discrete
codes [15]. Although these codes may preserve useful latent information, they are neither explicitly grounded in the original item
metadata nor naturally aligned with the pretrained LLM vocabulary. Consequently, their semantic content is difficult to inspect or
quantify, and their integration often requires vocabulary expansion,

Abstract
Modern industrial recommender systems (RecSys) increasingly
adopt Transformer-based sequence models, with an emerging paradigm that frames recommendation as next-token prediction over a
unified monolithic user sequence. However, collapsing heterogeneous data sources – such as long-term user behaviors and real-time
serving events – into a single monolithic token stream that obscures
their distinct causal roles and temporal characteristics, leading to
inefficient modeling and elevated training and serving costs.
We propose TransX, a production-oriented encoder–decoder
architecture that reformulates recommendation as a sequence-tosequence action transduction problem. TransX explicitly decouples behavior-stream modeling from serving-event modeling and
conditions next-action decoding on scalable cross-attention between nearline behavior encodings and real-time serving representations. To enable low-latency, high-QPS deployment, TransX is
co-designed with an amortized serving strategy that combines incremental behavior encoding with per-request key–value caching,
rendering serving latency insensitive to behavior sequence length.
Extensive offline experiments and large-scale online A/B tests on
LinkedIn’s recommender systems show that TransX consistently
outperforms state-of-the-art DLRMs and sequential baselines, and
delivers substantial CTR lift (+6.0%) and conversion gain (+4.4%)
while maintaining serving costs comparable to existing production
models where our co-designed serving strategy reduces online
computation by approximately 80%.

Introduction

Industrial recommender systems (RecSys) are the primary engine
of user engagement for online platforms, requiring models that
can process billions of events daily with sub-second latency [23].
For the past decade, Deep Learning Recommendation Models (DLRMs) have dominated this space by leveraging human-engineered
features and sparse interactions [19, 36]. While effective, DLRMs
are fundamentally constrained by their limited ability to ingest
ultra-long, heterogeneous behavioral histories, often relying on
static aggregations that lose the rich temporal semantics of user
intent.
Motivated by the success of Large Language Models (LLMs), recent work has begun to reformulate recommendation via sequence
transduction or generative modeling [10, 16, 29]. In this emerging
paradigm, user-system interactions are sequentialized into token
streams, and the recommendation task is treated as a sequence
transduction problem – mapping an input sequence to an output
sequence of user actions [13, 37] – or next-item generation problem
[8, 22, 35]. This shift allows models to scale their capacity with
increased sequence length, tokenization complexity, and compute,
reducing the reliance on manual feature engineering in favor of
automated, Transformer-based feature interactions.
Despite these advances, many architectures in this emerging
paradigm adopt a "monolithic" design that closely mirrors standard
LLM training [16, 29]. Specifically, they collapse heterogeneous data
streams — including user historical behaviors and system serving
events (e.g., candidate exposures) — into a single unified token
sequence. While effective in some settings, this design introduces
two key limitations in many industrial recommender systems:
(1) Semantic conflation: it forces the model to treat heterogeneous data generation processes as semantically homogeneous,
obscuring the distinct causal and modeling roles of user historical behaviors versus system exposures in recommendation.

 KDD ’26, August 09–13, 2026, Jeju Island, Republic of Korea

(2) Computational inefficiency: collapsing the streams increases
sequence length and tokenization complexity, and requires reencoding the entire behavior prefix for each candidate request,
leading to substantial redundant computation.
Our work aims to address these limitations in settings where heterogeneous signals and serving efficiency are both critical.
First part of our solution: architecture innovation. To address these
challenges, we first introduce TransX, an architecture built on the
principle of Action Transduction via Stream Crossing. We observe that recommendation is naturally a dual-stream process: (i)
a serving-event stream, in which the system selects and presents
a slate of candidate items to the user, and (ii) a behavior stream,
which captures the user’s broader activity across the platform, including both responses to recommendations (e.g. clicks or likes)
and organic actions (e.g. searches or profile views). TransX
models a user’s response as the interaction between their longterm behavioral trajectory and the system’s immediate serving
slate. And motivated by the distinct generative processes and statistical roles of these streams, it explicitly separates them using an
encoder–decoder architecture The encoder processes the behavior stream to learn latent user intent, while the decoder performs
parallel action transduction, mapping the crossing of the behavior
stream and the serving slate into a discrete vocabulary of action
tokens (e.g. click, view, dismiss).
Second part of our solution: model-infrastructure co-design. Recognizing that large-scale recommendation in industry is as much
about infrastructure as it is about modeling. We co-design TransX
with a streaming sequence-to-sequence training pipeline that substantially increases training throughput. By performing the behavior encoding nearline and caching the resulting representations,
we shift the bulk of the model’s computational cost away from
the critical serving path. At request time, only a lightweight crossattention "crossing" and action decoding are performed. We also
incorporate KV caching and parallel decoding into the design to
further reduce serving latency. Together, they allow TransX to scale
to 180-day behavior windows while maintaining an online serving
cost comparable to traditional DLRMs in LinkedIn’s large-scale
deployment.
Real-world impact. To validate TransX’s production impact, we
conducted extensive experiments on LinkedIn’s social recommendation dataset where TransX consistently outperforms both traditional DLRMs and recent sequence modeling baselines under
a similar compute budget. In large-scale online A/B experiments,
TransX delivers the largest CTR lift observed in recent years for a
major social recommendation application in LinkedIn.

Abstract
Stale recommendations are a pervasive challenge and a leading
source of user complaints on large-scale content platforms. Items
lose relevance through two primary mechanisms: supersession,
where emerging updates render prior coverage stale, and relevance
decay, where an item’s informational value naturally diminishes
over its lifecycle. Traditional countermeasures serve as crude proxies: age cutoffs poorly reflect actual relevance loss, while engagement heuristics rely on lagging signals, broadly exposing users to
stale content before the system adapts.
We present SDF (Supersession-Decay Filtering), a staleness
filtering system fully deployed in Google Discover, a personalized
recommendation feed with hundreds of millions of daily and billions of monthly active users. SDF targets both mechanisms with
complementary filters, each powered by a learned model: a relational staleness model that detects supersession between item pairs,
and a predicted traffic ratio (PTR) model that forecasts relevance decay from the item’s content, trained on lifetime visit traffic. Applied
via disjunction upstream of the ranking stage, SDF prunes stale
candidates, measurably reducing downstream serving costs. Online experiments demonstrate that these filters significantly reduce
the prevalence of stale content while improving user engagement.
Over a two-year production deployment, user-filed staleness reports (in-product user feedback) declined by 54.9% relative to the
pre-deployment baseline, establishing SDF as a robust and scalable
paradigm for resolving content staleness at industrial scale.

Introduction

Recommender systems are inherently time-sensitive. They surface
content against an evolving notion of relevance, and when this
evaluation lags reality, items become stale: they continue to surface
despite no longer reflecting the current state of the underlying
topic. In large-scale recommender systems like Google Discover,
staleness is a pervasive challenge and a primary source of user
dissatisfaction. Staleness is not a monolithic problem. Items lose
relevance through distinct mechanisms that dictate both how staleness manifests and how it must be detected. This work addresses
two primary dimensions:
Supersession. An item abruptly becomes stale when a newly arriving item advances the underlying topic. For example, an early
bulletin reporting that “Queen Elizabeth II is under medical supervision” was superseded within hours by the announcement of her
passing; similarly, an early report that “Ohtani is weighing offers
from multiple teams” was rendered stale the moment his signing
with the Dodgers was announced. The staleness signal here is relational rather than absolute. Because only updates that contradict,
supersede, or shift the narrative render an older item stale, detection requires comparing item pairs, not just by publication time
(Figure 1, top).
Relevance decay. An item naturally loses informational value over
its lifecycle, driven by its own content rather than supersession. A
guide to “tonight’s meteor shower” is highly useful for one evening
before its relevance sharply drops, and a heartwarming local clip
naturally fades without any follow-up. The staleness signal here is
intrinsic to the item, tied directly to its intended lifespan (Figure 1,
bottom).
Traditional countermeasures address neither aspect effectively.
Time-based ranking demotes rather than removes stale items, forcing users to still scroll past them. Hand-tuned age cutoffs are
coarse and heavily rely on publication time; a long cutoff still
serves stale items, while a short one drops useful evergreen content.

Abstract
Positional encoding is a fundamental component of
Transformer-based generative recommendation models, where
user histories are modeled as autoregressive item sequences.
Most positional encoding methods are inherited from natural
language processing and mainly represent discrete item order.
However, recommendation sequences go beyond ordered lists, as
timestamps and temporal eﬀects also shape item relations. Our
work is motivated by a real-world food delivery and instant
retail recommendation system, where user behavior exhibits
multi-level temporal regularities, including recency eﬀects, mealtime peaks, weekday–weekend shis, and promotion-driven
traﬃc bursts. Existing methods partially address this issue
through timestamp features, interval embeddings, decay
functions, or aention biases, but they usually inject
heterogeneous temporal signals through a uniﬁed representation
or a single modeling pathway, making it diﬃcult to distinguish
broad temporal dynamics from local order cues. To address this
limitation, we propose Decoupled Temporal Encoding (DTE),
a lightweight framework for generative recommendation. DTE
separates temporal dynamics from order information through
two complementary modules: a personalized macro-temporal
module that injects compact temporal primitives into item
embeddings, and a time-gated micro-sequential module that
introduces relative-order bias only when interactions are
temporally dense. DTE is also parameter-eﬃcient and
deployment-friendly, allowing easy integration into existing
systems. Oﬄine experiments on public and industrial datasets
demonstrate DTE’s superior performance. Online A/B tests
further show improvements of +1.8% Click-through Rate (CTR)
and +3.0% Revenue Per Mille (RPM) with only +0.3% serving

latency overhead over the baseline positional encoding scheme.
DTE has been deployed to the full Shangou ad recommendation
traﬃc in the Taobao App since January 2026, highlighting the
practical value of decoupling macro-temporal context from
sequential order in real-world generative recommendation.

Generative recommendation has emerged as a powerful
paradigm for modern recommender systems [5-10]. It represents
user interaction histories as item sequences and reformulates
next-item recommendation as an autoregressive sequence
generation task. Compared with traditional candidate-scoring
frameworks, this paradigm provides a natural way to model
evolving user interests and has shown promising advantages in
several real-world applications [5, 7, 10]. Similar to large
language models (LLMs), Transformer architectures serve as a
core building block of generative recommendation, where selfattention is used to capture complex dependencies among
historical items. However, self-attention alone is permutationinvariant and does not explicitly encode sequence order, making
positional encoding an indispensable component for
Transformer-based generative recommendation [4]. Commonly
used positional encoding schemes, such as sinusoidal
embeddings [11] and Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE) [12],
were originally developed for large language models (LLM) and
are mainly designed to represent discrete token positions. In
recommendation scenarios, however, user behavior sequences
are not merely ordered lists: their timestamps contain rich
continuous-time semantics that also shape item relations and
user intent. These observations highlight the importance of
temporal effects and motivate the development of time-aware
positional encoding methods for generative recommendation.
Specifically, this work is motivated by, and initially designed
for, the food delivery and instant retail recommendation system.
In this practical scenario, user behavior exhibits multi-level
temporal effects that are highly relevant to recommendation.
First, recent interactions often carry stronger predictive value,
reflecting a clear recency effect in user intent. Second, demand
repeatedly concentrates around meal-related periods such as
lunch and dinner, indicating strong intra-day periodicity. Third,
user preferences and consumption needs may shift between
weekdays and weekends, suggesting weekly temporal patterns: a
user may frequently order prepared meals during weekday lunch
hours, while showing weaker delivery demand or stronger
grocery-oriented consumption on weekends. Finally, promotions,
holidays, or operational events may induce short-term traffic
surges, leading to bursty temporal deviations from regular
behavior. These observations suggest that timestamps are not
merely auxiliary context features, they encode multiple temporal
effects that are essential for understanding evolving user intent.
Meanwhile, we further highlight that such temporal effects
complement, rather than replace, sequential order. Order
information characterizes how user behaviors unfold. This
distinction is especially important for temporally dense
interactions, where relative order can still reveal meaningful
item relationships. It is thus of importance here to explicitly
incorporate both temporal and order effects when designing
position encoding method.
To account for temporal effects, existing time-aware
recommendation methods propose to inject time features,
interval embeddings, or attention biases into sequential models
[15–17]. While useful, such approaches often encode
heterogeneous temporal effects in a unified representation,

ABSTRACT
Sequential models have become increasingly popular in powering
personalized recommendation systems over the past several years.
These approaches traditionally model a user’s actions on a website
as a sequence to predict the user’s next action. While theoretically
simplistic, these models are quite challenging to deploy in production, commonly requiring streaming infrastructure to reflect the
latest user activity and potentially managing mutable data for encoding a user’s hidden state. Here we introduce PinnerFormer, a
user representation trained to predict a user’s future long-term engagement using a sequential model of a user’s recent actions. Unlike
prior approaches, we adapt our modeling to a batch infrastructure
via our new dense all-action loss, modeling long-term future actions
instead of next action prediction. We show that by doing so, we
significantly close the gap between batch user embeddings that
are generated once a day and realtime user embeddings generated
whenever a user takes an action. We describe our design decisions
via extensive offline experimentation and ablations and validate the
efficacy of our approach in A/B experiments showing substantial
improvements in Pinterest’s user retention and engagement when
comparing PinnerFormer against our previous user representation.
PinnerFormer is deployed in production as of Fall 2021.
